rv.q: All three actors are very fine but the great virtue ofthis production is that it is more than a showpiece for stars and highlightsMamet's ability to write a far-reaching fable about thejungle ofAmerican capitalism.
I don't think I have ever seen the tentatively cathartic, forgiving hug between the guilty Donny and the shattered Bob more movingly registered.
And yet this production doesn't quite fire on all cylinders: it's somehow too self-conscious.
This is a shaggy-dog story that snaps, bites, gets pretty brutal and finally draws blood before it lies down quietly and with an unexpected tenderness.
This starry revival boasts three fine performances and moments of abrasive comedy, even if it takes a while to come to the boil.
At the moment, however, it’s all enjoyable enough but a bit dime-a-dozen.
The trouble, I found, was that while all three men are individually excellent, they don't gel enough to really excavate their characters' hidden depths.
It looks like a Mamet, sounds like a Mamet but a strain of British restraint and rather disappointingly lukewarm evening.
Some hold this play to be a 20th-century American classic. I hesitate to go that far.
On paper it all sounds grey, miserable and petty. On stage it's magnificent, multicoloured, vast and tragic.
It’s a memorable evening and you’ll experience some extraordinary acting from Goodman and Sturridge in a powerful play.
Individually, each of these characters is an engrossing portrait, but they don’t slot together.
But it all needs a bit more savagery.
But you feel it deeply for these small-time crooks.
Capitalism in the form ofavarice and opportunism, the desperation ofsociety's bottom feeders and the unacknowledged need for companionship lie at the heart of this immense play.

cn.t: Mamet's 40-year-old drama remains punchy and relevant, featuring three strong performances from its star trio, though the production takes time to gel and sometimes feels more like a showcase for celebrity talent than a cohesive ensemble piece.
